hints: Distance and velocity, no time: write the acceleration as v dv/dx and separate the variables.
worded:
1. Acceleration depends on v, and the question links v with distance. So use a = v dv/dx.

2. v dv/dx = −k√v gives √v dv = −k dx.

3. Integrating √v from u down to 0 gives ⅔u^(3/2), which equals k times the distance. So the distance is 2u^(3/2)/3k. (B)

4. Units check: k has units m^½ s^(−3/2), and u^(3/2)/k comes out in metres. Option (C) and (D) have k in the numerator and fail this check.
conventional:

$$v\frac{dv}{dx} = - k\sqrt{v}\  \Rightarrow \ \sqrt{v}\, dv = - k\, dx.$$

$$\int_{u}^{0}v^{1/2}\, dv = - k\int_{0}^{s}dx\  \Rightarrow \  - \frac{2}{3}u^{3/2} = - ks\  \Rightarrow \ s = \frac{2u^{3/2}}{3k}.$$
mistakes: Use a = v dv/dx (for distance), not a = dv/dt (which gives the stopping time, 2√u/k).
